title: Wondering and asking 'why?'
keyIdea: Scientists start by wondering. You notice something, ask a why, how or what-if question, and have a go at a guess. Then you find out by looking closely, trying it, or asking someone. A guess does not have to be right. It is how finding out begins.

kid: Look at a snail. Do you wonder why it has a shell? That wonder is a question. Questions often start with why, how or what if.
Next, have a go at a guess. Maybe the shell keeps it safe. Your guess can be wrong. That is fine. A guess helps you start.
Then find out. You can look closely. You can try it and see. Or you can ask a grown-up, or look in a book.
Some things fool us. Shiny foil looks like it should stick to a magnet. But when you try it, it does not. Trying it showed you the real answer.
adult: This is the first step of scientific inquiry. A child notices something, asks a question, offers a guess and then looks for evidence. In England, Development Matters (2023) sets out what 3 and 4 year olds do. They use all their senses to explore natural materials. They explore how things work. They explore and talk about forces they can feel, such as a magnet's pull. In Communication and Language, they learn to understand why questions. The Characteristics of Effective Learning add having their own ideas, making predictions and testing them. In the US, the Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework goal P-SCI 4 says the child asks a question, gathers information, and makes predictions. At 36 to 48 months that means simple questions, adults as the main source of answers, and simple predictions with support.

Young children ask a great many questions. Chouinard (2007) recorded children aged 1 to 5 asking dozens of information-seeking questions an hour in everyday talk with parents. Frazier, Gelman and Wellman (2009) found that preschoolers notice when they get a non-answer: after a real explanation they tended to agree or ask a follow-up, but after a non-answer they often asked again or offered their own explanation. So "why" is usually a genuine request for a cause, not stalling.

Common mistakes: brushing off why questions with "because it is", which teaches that questions are a nuisance. Answering so fast that the child never makes a guess of their own. Treating a wrong guess as a failure, so the child stops guessing. A common slip in the science itself is believing that all shiny or metal things stick to a magnet. Only some metals, mainly iron and steel, are pulled; aluminium foil is not.

In the lab your child taps things in a garden to wonder about them. Then they sort asking sentences from telling ones. They make a guess before they hear each answer. They test seven things on a magnet, and they are stopped if they try to sort a thing before testing it. Last, they match questions to a way to find out: look, try it, or ask.

familyTip: When your child asks why, try "What do you think?" before you answer, and welcome any guess. Then find out together: look closely, try it, or look it up. A fridge magnet and a few things from a drawer make a quick test of the shiny-foil surprise.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: wonder about things in a garden, sort asking from telling, guess first, test things on a magnet, and choose how to find out.

practice.prompt: Which one is a wonder question?
practice.hint: A question asks something. Look for why, how or what if.
practice.explain: "Why do birds sing?" asks for a reason. The other two tell you a thing.

practice.prompt: You test {n} things on a magnet. 2 of them stick. How many do not stick?
practice.hint: Start with the {n} things and take away the 2 that stick.
practice.explain: {n} take away 2 is {=n-2}. Testing each one showed you which stick.

practice.prompt: Will my toy boat float? What is the best way to find out?
choices: Put it in water and see
practice.hint: Can you try this one yourself?
practice.explain: You can try it! Putting the boat in water shows you if it floats.

practice.prompt: You asked {n} why questions at the park and 1 more at home. How many why questions did you ask?
practice.hint: You asked {n}, then 1 more. Count on 1 from {n}.
practice.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1}. Every question is a chance to find out.

pool.prompt: Your guess was wrong. Is that OK?
choices: Yes. A guess helps you start.
pool.hint: Do scientists always guess right the first time?
pool.explain: A guess does not have to be right. You guess, then you find out the real answer.

pool.prompt: Which thing will stick to a magnet?
pool.explain: The paper clip is steel, so it sticks. Cloth and plastic do not.

pool.prompt: Shiny foil does not stick to a magnet. Why?
choices: Foil is not iron or steel
pool.hint: Shiny is not the thing that matters. What is foil made of?
pool.explain: Magnets pull iron and steel. Foil is a different metal, so it does not stick.

pool.prompt: A ladybird sits on a leaf in front of you. How many spots has it got? How can you find out?
pool.hint: Can you see the spots? Then you do not need to ask.
pool.explain: You can see the spots, so look closely and count them.

pool.prompt: Which word often starts a wonder question?
pool.hint: Which word asks for a reason?
pool.explain: "Why" asks for a reason. How and what if start wonder questions too.

pool.prompt: Where do penguins live? You have never seen one. How can you find out?
choices: Ask a grown-up or look in a book
pool.hint: Penguins are far away. Who or what could tell you?
pool.explain: You cannot see penguins from here, so ask someone or look in a book.

pool.prompt: You had {n} wonder questions. You found out the answer to 1. How many are still to find out?
pool.hint: Take the 1 you found out away from {n}.
pool.explain: {n} take away 1 is {=n-1}. Keep looking, trying and asking!

pool.prompt: Tom asks "Why?" lots of times. What do you think?
pool.hint: How do we find out new things?
pool.explain: Asking why is how you find out. It is a good thing to do.

pool.prompt: {n} things stuck to the magnet. You test 1 more steel pin. It sticks too. How many stuck now?
pool.hint: Steel sticks, so count on 1 from {n}.
pool.explain: {n} and 1 more is {=n+1}. The steel pin stuck, like the other steel things.
